question: When national data protection regulators ask the European-level board to review a case, how are they supposed to send over the facts and their reasoning?
Can a charity or advocacy group file a privacy complaint for me and seek compensation for me if a company mishandled my personal information?
After the European data protection board settles a disagreement between national privacy regulators about my complaint, how long does the regulator I complained to have to issue its final decision?
Is there an official public list where I can check which organizations are approved to issue data protection certifications, and which companies outside the EU have earned one?
What is the biggest fine a company could get if it ignores people's requests to see or delete their data, or sends their information abroad without proper safeguards?
If our company has a data leak and we have to report it to the privacy regulator, what details does the report need to include?
Can my business use an industry-approved set of rules or a official security certificate to show we're keeping our customers' data properly protected?
Who gives the European Commission advice on what standards a certification must meet before a company can be approved to certify data protection compliance?
If a country has several different data protection offices, who speaks for them together at the European level?
How will the European Commission find out about a country's own workplace data protection rules, and by when did countries have to report them?
If I work for a company and can see customers' personal information, am I allowed to use it in ways my boss hasn't told me to?
If a company got my details from someone else and later wants to use them for a new reason, do they have to tell me first?

If my country's data protection regulator wants to approve a company's internal rules for sharing personal data across its branches in different countries, does it have to get an opinion from the European-level group of regulators first?
What does the EU look at when deciding whether a country outside Europe protects people's personal data well enough for companies to send data there?
When I'm building a new app that handles customers' personal details, what privacy protections do I have to build in from the start and keep up while it's running?
If a company gets my details from someone else rather than from me, what do they have to tell me about who they are, why they're using my data, and who they're sharing it with?
If my company has offices in several EU countries, how do we work out which one counts as our main base for data protection purposes?
If my country's legal system doesn't allow data protection authorities to issue fines themselves, how can a penalty for a privacy violation still be imposed?
If I keep sending the data protection regulator the same request over and over, can they ask me to pay or just ignore me, and who has to prove I'm being unreasonable?

If my company is based outside Europe and has appointed someone to act for us there, can regulators or customers contact that person instead of us about how we handle personal information?
If I work in a job with a confidentiality duty, like a lawyer or doctor, can my country limit what a data protection regulator is allowed to access or demand from me?
If my online shop is based outside Europe but sells to people living in Europe or tracks what they do on my website, do I have to follow the EU's data protection rules?
Does the age rule for a child's consent to online services change how contracts with minors work under my country's normal laws?
At what age can a teenager sign up for an online service and agree to the use of their data without a parent saying yes?
If someone hacks into a company's system or an employee accidentally sends my details to the wrong person, does that count as an official data breach?
Can my employer fire me or punish me for doing my job as the company's data protection officer, and who am I supposed to report to?
Can I still publish an article, artwork, or academic piece that mentions real people, or do data privacy rules limit what I can say?

If a government agency asks a company for someone's information as part of an official investigation, does that agency count as one of the parties the company has to tell people their data was shared with?
When a European data protection board settles a disagreement between national privacy regulators, where can I find out what it decided?
